lesson.text: You cannot lock your way to security.

The law requires "appropriate technical AND organizational measures" to keep personal data safe — TOMs. You built both in the Town Hall. The word that matters is AND: they are not alternatives, and neither is sufficient alone.

TWO KINDS OF MEASURE

TECHNICAL MEASURES — the hardware and software barriers. Encryption, access controls, vaults, keys, network segmentation, backups. They act on the SYSTEM. (The Iron Vault; the Brass Key.)

ORGANIZATIONAL MEASURES — the policies and procedures governing how the tools are used and by whom. Access policies, staff training, role separation, logging, incident procedures, vetting. They act on PEOPLE. (The Shift Roster; the Countersign; the Logbook.)
The reason you need both is that they defend against DIFFERENT ATTACKERS — this is the lesson of the three thieves.

WHO EACH MEASURE STOPS

THE OUTSIDER (no right to the data) — stopped by TECHNICAL measures. A vault keeps out those who were never allowed in.

THE OFF-HOURS INSIDER (a right, misused outside its bounds) — stopped by ORGANIZATIONAL rules. A key that only works 8-to-5 governs the trusted.

THE AUTHORIZED ABUSER (every right, wrong purpose) — no barrier stops him; he belongs there. Only ACCOUNTABILITY reaches him: audit logs that record who did what, so misuse is seen, deterred, and provable after the fact.

That third figure is why audit logging is not bureaucracy. You cannot always PREVENT the trusted; you can always ACCOUNT for them. This is the accountability principle in law — not only must you protect data, you must be able to DEMONSTRATE that you did.

DEFENCE IN DEPTH — THEY INTERLOCK

Measures are layered, and they depend on each other. Separation of duties (two people to authorize) means nothing if there is no lock on the door — the two people simply stand before an open vault. Access control means nothing if the key never expires. A log means nothing if no one ever reads it. Security is not a pile of measures; it is measures that INTERLOCK, each covering another's blind spot.

One more legal anchor: the law asks for measures "APPROPRIATE to the risk." More sensitive data and greater potential harm demand stronger, more layered measures — the Master Tax Ledger earns a vault, a roster, a countersign, AND a logbook precisely because a leak ruins lives. A cabbage-stall's tally does not. Proportion again: enough, not everything.

quiz.q: Classify the measure: "The vault key only functions between 8 AM and 5 PM."
explain: The key and vault are technical — but a RULE about when a tool may be used isn't itself the hardware.
Exactly — the LOCK is technical; the RULE about WHEN it may be used is organizational, a policy governing how the tool is used. TOMs often pair a technical tool with an organizational rule about it.
This is very much a measure — a schedule restriction on access is one of the most common organizational controls there is.

quiz.q: A thief with no connection to the Town Hall tries to grab the ledger. Which measure stops him?
explain: Logging records what happened — it doesn't stop the outsider from getting in, it only proves it afterward.
Exactly — an outsider is stopped by a barrier: he was never authorized, so a lock does the job. Organizational measures govern the trusted, not the stranger.
Training shapes how authorized staff behave — it has no effect on someone with no legitimate access at all.

quiz.q: A clerk with full, legitimate daytime access reads a neighbour's debts out of pure curiosity. Which measure best addresses this?
explain: He's already inside the hours the lock permits — a heavier lock doesn't change who's allowed to turn the key.
He's browsing during his own authorized hours — narrowing the schedule further doesn't touch this specific abuse.

Exactly — he has every right to be there at that hour with that key; no barrier or schedule excludes him. Accountability (a record of who accessed what, why) deters and catches authorized abuse. You can't always prevent the trusted; you can always account for them.

quiz.q: The Mayor requires two officials to co-authorize emptying the vault, but no one ever installed a lock. What's the flaw?
choices: Separation of duties without a technical barrier is theatre — the door is open
explain: The number of required signatures isn't the problem — the missing barrier underneath them is.

Exactly — organizational controls need technical ones beneath them. Countersigning an unlocked door stops no one. Defence in depth means the measures INTERLOCK; a control with nothing under it is decoration.
It is not secure — two people solemnly authorizing access to an unlocked vault stops absolutely no one.

quiz.q: Why does the Master Tax Ledger get a vault, roster, countersign AND logbook, while the cabbage-stall's tally gets none of it?
choices: Measures must be APPROPRIATE to the risk
explain: The Mayor's standing has nothing to do with it — the ledger's contents, not its owner's title, drive the requirement.

Exactly — the law scales required measures to the sensitivity of the data and the harm a breach would cause. High-harm data earns layered protection; trivial data does not. Proportion, not paranoia — enough, not everything.
Cost isn't the deciding factor here — even a free measure would be overkill on data whose exposure harms no one.
